lessons.title: Multiple Testing & False Discovery Rate
lessons.interviewAnswer: When many hypotheses are tested, false positives accumulate. Family-wise methods such as Bonferroni control any false positive; FDR methods such as Benjamini–Hochberg control the expected proportion among discoveries.
keyPoints: More tests → more opportunities for false positives.
FWER and FDR are different guarantees.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Multiple Testing & False Discovery Rate make?
How would you validate or debug Multiple Testing & False Discovery Rate in practice?

lessons.title: Effect Size vs Statistical Significance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Statistical significance asks whether an effect is hard to explain by noise under a null; effect size asks whether the magnitude is practically meaningful. Large samples can make tiny effects significant.
keyPoints: Report magnitude and uncertainty, not p-value alone.
Practical significance depends on costs/base rates.
Confidence intervals communicate plausible effect ranges.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Effect Size vs Statistical Significance make?
How would you validate or debug Effect Size vs Statistical Significance in practice?

lessons.title: ANOVA & Comparing Multiple Groups
lessons.interviewAnswer: ANOVA tests whether group means differ more than expected from within-group variability under model assumptions. A significant omnibus test does not say which groups differ, so post-hoc comparisons require care.
keyPoints: Assumptions include independence and model-specific variance/error structure.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does ANOVA & Comparing Multiple Groups make?
How would you validate or debug ANOVA & Comparing Multiple Groups in practice?

lessons.title: Chi-square Tests for Categorical Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: Chi-square tests compare observed categorical counts with counts expected under a null such as independence. They operate on counts, not percentages detached from sample size.
keyPoints: Expected cell counts matter for approximation quality.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Chi-square Tests for Categorical Data make?
How would you validate or debug Chi-square Tests for Categorical Data in practice?

lessons.title: Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size
lessons.interviewAnswer: Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a specified size when it truly exists. Sample-size planning links baseline variance/rate, significance level, desired power and minimum detectable effect.
keyPoints: Power is defined relative to an alternative effect size.
Low power produces noisy, inconclusive experiments.

How would you validate or debug Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size in practice?

lessons.title: Bayesian Updating: Prior, Likelihood & Posterior
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bayesian inference updates prior beliefs with evidence through the likelihood to produce a posterior distribution. The posterior represents uncertainty about parameters after observing data.
keyPoints: Posterior predictive checks validate consequences of the model.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Bayesian Updating: Prior, Likelihood & Posterior make?
How would you validate or debug Bayesian Updating: Prior, Likelihood & Posterior in practice?

lessons.title: Conjugate Priors
lessons.interviewAnswer: A conjugate prior is chosen so the posterior remains in the same distribution family, giving closed-form updates. It is useful pedagogically and computationally for simple models, though modern Bayesian modeling often uses numerical inference.
keyPoints: Beta-Binomial and Normal-Normal are classic pairs.
Convenience should not override sensible prior modeling.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Conjugate Priors make?
How would you validate or debug Conjugate Priors in practice?

lessons.title: Credible Intervals vs Confidence Intervals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Bayesian credible interval is a probability statement about a parameter under the posterior; a frequentist confidence interval is a procedure that covers the fixed parameter at a stated long-run frequency.
keyPoints: Interpretations differ even when numerical intervals look similar.
Frequentist coverage is about repeated procedures.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Credible Intervals vs Confidence Intervals make?
How would you validate or debug Credible Intervals vs Confidence Intervals in practice?

lessons.title: MCMC & Posterior Sampling
lessons.interviewAnswer: MCMC constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior, letting us approximate expectations when closed-form inference is unavailable. Diagnostics are essential because samples can be correlated or chains may not mix.
keyPoints: Burn-in/warmup is not a substitute for convergence diagnostics.
Check multiple chains, R-hat and effective sample size.
Posterior samples enable arbitrary derived quantities.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does MCMC & Posterior Sampling make?
How would you validate or debug MCMC & Posterior Sampling in practice?

lessons.title: Hierarchical / Multilevel Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: Hierarchical models partially pool related groups, sharing statistical strength while allowing group-specific effects. They are often better than either one global estimate or completely independent estimates for sparse groups.
keyPoints: Partial pooling reduces noisy extreme group estimates.
Useful for stores, regions, users or experiments.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Hierarchical / Multilevel Models make?
How would you validate or debug Hierarchical / Multilevel Models in practice?

lessons.title: Posterior Predictive Checks & Bayesian Model Criticism
lessons.interviewAnswer: Posterior predictive checks simulate data from the fitted model and compare it with observed patterns. They test whether the model can reproduce important features, not whether the model is “true.”
keyPoints: Choose discrepancy statistics tied to the use case.
Good fit on one summary can hide poor fit elsewhere.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Posterior Predictive Checks & Bayesian Model Criticism make?
How would you validate or debug Posterior Predictive Checks & Bayesian Model Criticism in practice?

lessons.title: Linear Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics
lessons.interviewAnswer: For inference, linear regression relies on assumptions about functional form, independent errors, variance structure and error distribution; for prediction, diagnostics still reveal misspecification, outliers and extrapolation risk.
keyPoints: Check leverage/influence, not just residual size.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Linear Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics make?
How would you validate or debug Linear Regression Assumptions & Diagnostics in practice?

lessons.title: Ridge, Lasso & Elastic Net
lessons.interviewAnswer: Ridge uses L2 regularization to shrink coefficients; Lasso uses L1 and can set coefficients exactly to zero; Elastic Net combines both, often helping with correlated features.
lessons.labGoal: See how L1/L2 regularization changes coefficients.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Ridge, Lasso & Elastic Net make?
How would you validate or debug Ridge, Lasso & Elastic Net in practice?

lessons.title: Polynomial Regression & Splines
lessons.interviewAnswer: Basis expansion lets linear models represent nonlinear relationships. High-degree global polynomials can behave badly at boundaries; splines build smoother local pieces joined at knots.
keyPoints: Model remains linear in coefficients despite nonlinear features.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Polynomial Regression & Splines make?
How would you validate or debug Polynomial Regression & Splines in practice?

lessons.title: Generalized Additive Models (GAMs)
lessons.interviewAnswer: GAMs add flexible smooth functions of individual predictors while retaining an additive, interpretable structure. They are useful when relationships are nonlinear but black-box complexity is unnecessary.
keyPoints: Additivity is interpretable but limits interactions unless added explicitly.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) make?
How would you validate or debug Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) in practice?

lessons.title: Poisson & Count Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Poisson regression models count outcomes with a log link and assumes the conditional variance equals the conditional mean. Overdispersion often motivates negative-binomial or quasi-likelihood alternatives.
keyPoints: Predictions are nonnegative through log link.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Poisson & Count Regression make?

lessons.title: Robust Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Robust regression reduces the influence of extreme residuals compared with squared-error OLS, using losses such as Huber or alternative estimators.
keyPoints: Differentiate data errors from valid heavy tails.
Robust loss changes influence, not the data itself.
Compare with quantile regression when conditional tails matter.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Robust Regression make?

lessons.title: Quantile Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Quantile regression estimates conditional quantiles rather than the conditional mean, making it useful for asymmetric distributions and questions about medians or tails.
keyPoints: Pinball/check loss targets a chosen quantile.
Different quantiles can have different predictor effects.
Useful for prediction intervals and tail planning.

lessons.title: Hierarchical Clustering
lessons.interviewAnswer: Hierarchical clustering repeatedly merges or splits clusters and produces a dendrogram. Linkage choice defines how inter-cluster distance is measured and can strongly change results.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Hierarchical Clustering make?

lessons.title: DBSCAN & Density-based Clustering
lessons.interviewAnswer: DBSCAN defines clusters as dense regions connected through neighborhoods, can identify noise points, and does not require a fixed number of clusters. It struggles when cluster densities vary strongly.
lessons.labGoal: Recover density-based clusters and noise points.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does DBSCAN & Density-based Clustering make?

lessons.title: Gaussian Mixture Models & EM
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Gaussian mixture models data as a weighted combination of Gaussian components and gives soft cluster probabilities. EM alternates between estimating component responsibilities and updating parameters.
keyPoints: Soft assignments differ from k-means hard labels.
Likelihood can favor complexity without regularization/model selection.
lessons.labGoal: Fit a Gaussian mixture and inspect soft memberships.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Gaussian Mixture Models & EM make?

lessons.title: t-SNE & UMAP for Visualization
lessons.interviewAnswer: t-SNE and UMAP create low-dimensional embeddings that emphasize neighborhood structure, mainly for exploration/visualization. Global distances and cluster sizes can be misleading, especially with t-SNE.
keyPoints: Do not treat 2D distance as ground truth.
Use PCA or task metrics alongside visualization.

lessons.title: Density Estimation & KDE
lessons.interviewAnswer: Density estimation approximates the underlying probability density. Kernel density estimation smooths observations with kernels; bandwidth is the critical bias–variance control.
keyPoints: Bandwidth too small overfits, too large oversmooths.
Useful for exploration/anomaly scoring in low dimension.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Density Estimation & KDE make?
How would you validate or debug Density Estimation & KDE in practice?

lessons.title: Randomized Experiment Design
lessons.interviewAnswer: A trustworthy experiment starts with a unit of randomization, eligibility criteria, treatment assignment, primary metric, guardrails and a pre-specified analysis plan. Randomization protects causal interpretation when implementation is correct.
keyPoints: Define exposure and sample ratio checks.
Primary metrics and guardrails should be decided before reading results.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Randomized Experiment Design make?

lessons.title: Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM)
lessons.interviewAnswer: SRM occurs when observed treatment/control counts differ unexpectedly from the planned allocation. It is a diagnostic red flag for assignment, logging, eligibility or exposure bugs, so effect estimates should not be trusted until explained.
keyPoints: Test assignment counts against expected proportions.
SRM can signal instrumentation or filtering bugs.
Do not “fix” SRM by reweighting blindly.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) make?
How would you validate or debug Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) in practice?

lessons.title: Variance Reduction & CUPED
lessons.interviewAnswer: CUPED uses pre-experiment covariates correlated with the outcome to reduce variance without changing the treatment effect expectation under valid conditions, increasing experiment sensitivity.

lessons.title: Sequential Testing, Peeking & Early Stopping
lessons.interviewAnswer: Repeatedly checking a fixed-horizon p-value and stopping when significant inflates false positives. Use precommitted horizons or valid sequential methods/alpha-spending when decisions are continuous.
keyPoints: Sequential designs can be valid when planned.
Operational urgency must not silently redefine statistics.

lessons.title: Metric Design: North Star, Driver & Guardrail Metrics
lessons.interviewAnswer: Good metrics reflect user/business value, respond to meaningful product changes, and resist gaming. Pair primary outcomes with driver diagnostics and guardrails for harmful side effects.
keyPoints: Avoid proxy metrics that are easy to move but disconnected from value.
Use guardrails for latency, quality, safety or churn.

lessons.title: Funnels & Conversion Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: A funnel measures progression through ordered steps. The main analytical challenge is defining eligibility, step ordering, time windows and denominators consistently rather than simply computing percentages.
keyPoints: Segment to locate where drop-off changes.

lessons.title: Cohort Retention Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: Retention should compare users at the same age since cohort entry, not raw calendar activity. Cohort tables reveal whether product changes affect long-term engagement across acquisition periods.
keyPoints: Choose retention event and time grain.
Account for right-censoring of recent cohorts.

lessons.title: Churn, Lifetime Value & Unit Economics
lessons.interviewAnswer: Churn and LTV metrics require explicit definitions of active, retained, revenue horizon and censoring. Predictive accuracy is secondary if the metric definition does not match the decision.
keyPoints: LTV can be historical or predictive.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Churn, Lifetime Value & Unit Economics make?

lessons.title: Potential Outcomes & Average Treatment Effects
lessons.interviewAnswer: Causal inference defines treatment effects through potential outcomes: what the same unit would experience under treatment versus control. Because both cannot be observed, identification requires randomization or assumptions/design.
keyPoints: Fundamental problem: one potential outcome is missing.
ATE, ATT and CATE answer different questions.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Potential Outcomes & Average Treatment Effects make?

lessons.title: Backdoor Adjustment & Confounding Control
lessons.interviewAnswer: A valid adjustment set blocks noncausal backdoor paths between treatment and outcome without conditioning on colliders or descendants that introduce bias. DAGs make these assumptions explicit.
keyPoints: Control confounders, not every available variable.
Conditioning on colliders can create associations.
Causal graph is an assumptions tool.

lessons.title: Propensity Scores, Matching & Weighting
lessons.interviewAnswer: The propensity score is the probability of treatment given observed covariates. Matching or inverse-probability weighting can balance observed confounders, but cannot repair unmeasured confounding or poor overlap.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Propensity Scores, Matching & Weighting make?
How would you validate or debug Propensity Scores, Matching & Weighting in practice?

lessons.title: Difference-in-Differences
lessons.interviewAnswer: Difference-in-differences compares outcome changes over time between treated and control groups. Its key identifying assumption is that, absent treatment, their trends would have evolved in parallel.

followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Difference-in-Differences make?

lessons.title: Instrumental Variables
lessons.interviewAnswer: An instrumental variable affects treatment, is independent of unmeasured outcome causes under assumptions, and affects the outcome only through treatment. IV can identify causal effects when confounding remains, but valid instruments are hard to justify.
keyPoints: Often estimates a local effect for compliers.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Instrumental Variables make?

lessons.title: Regression Discontinuity
lessons.interviewAnswer: RDD exploits a treatment rule that changes at a cutoff. Units just above and below the threshold can be comparable if they cannot precisely manipulate the running variable and potential outcomes vary smoothly at the cutoff.
keyPoints: Do not extrapolate local effects broadly without justification.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Regression Discontinuity make?

lessons.title: Synthetic Control
lessons.interviewAnswer: Synthetic control builds a weighted combination of untreated units that reproduces the treated unit’s pre-treatment trajectory, then uses post-treatment divergence as an estimated effect.
keyPoints: Useful for one/few treated aggregate units.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Synthetic Control make?

lessons.title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects & Uplift Modeling
lessons.interviewAnswer: Heterogeneous treatment-effect models estimate how intervention effects differ across units. The target is incremental impact, not outcome probability, so ordinary response prediction can rank the wrong people.
keyPoints: CATE/uplift differs from propensity to respond.
Evaluate policy value and uplift curves carefully.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Heterogeneous Treatment Effects & Uplift Modeling make?

lessons.title: Trend, Seasonality, Cycles & Remainder
lessons.interviewAnswer: A time series can contain trend, seasonal patterns, longer cycles and irregular remainder. I identify these structures before selecting a model because validation and feature construction depend on them.
keyPoints: Seasonality has a known calendar frequency; cycles need not.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Trend, Seasonality, Cycles & Remainder make?

lessons.title: Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage
lessons.interviewAnswer: Lag and rolling features summarize past information, but they must be constructed using only data available at prediction time. Centered windows or post-outcome aggregates silently leak the future.
keyPoints: Use the same pipeline in backtests and production.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Lags, Rolling Windows & Leakage make?

lessons.title: Naive, Seasonal-Naive & Drift Baselines
lessons.interviewAnswer: Forecasting should start with naive baselines. Last-value, seasonal-naive and drift forecasts often perform surprisingly well; a complex model is useful only if it beats the baseline out-of-sample.
keyPoints: Baseline defines whether complexity adds value.
lessons.labGoal: Build naive and seasonal-naive forecasts before complex models.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Naive, Seasonal-Naive & Drift Baselines make?

lessons.title: Classical Decomposition & STL
lessons.interviewAnswer: Decomposition separates trend, seasonal and remainder components. STL uses local regression and allows flexible changing seasonality, making it valuable for exploration, deseasonalization and anomaly diagnosis.
keyPoints: STL supports robust fitting to reduce outlier influence.

lessons.title: Dynamic Regression / ARIMAX
lessons.interviewAnswer: Dynamic regression combines external predictors with time-series error structure. It is useful when known drivers such as price, holidays or weather explain demand but residuals remain autocorrelated.

lessons.title: State-Space Models & Kalman Filtering
lessons.interviewAnswer: State-space models represent an evolving hidden state and an observation process. The Kalman filter recursively updates Gaussian linear state estimates as new observations arrive, enabling smoothing, missing-data handling and online forecasting.

Many forecasting models have state-space forms.

lessons.title: Multiple & Complex Seasonalities
lessons.interviewAnswer: Series such as hourly traffic can have daily, weekly and annual patterns. Models may use Fourier terms, dynamic harmonic regression, TBATS, boosted trees or neural approaches rather than a single seasonal period.
keyPoints: Calendar effects differ from smooth seasonality.
Long seasonal periods make naive one-hot approaches expensive.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Multiple & Complex Seasonalities make?

lessons.title: Intermittent Demand Forecasting
lessons.interviewAnswer: Intermittent demand contains many zeros with irregular positive events. Standard smooth forecasts can be biased; Croston-style methods separately model demand size and inter-arrival intervals.

followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Intermittent Demand Forecasting make?

lessons.title: Hierarchical & Grouped Forecast Reconciliation
lessons.interviewAnswer: When forecasts exist at product, region and total levels, independently trained models can be incoherent. Reconciliation adjusts forecasts so aggregation constraints are satisfied while preserving accuracy as much as possible.
keyPoints: Bottom-up, top-down and optimal reconciliation differ.
Hierarchy can be crossed/grouped, not only a tree.
Accuracy should be assessed across levels.

How would you validate or debug Hierarchical & Grouped Forecast Reconciliation in practice?

lessons.title: Prediction Intervals & Probabilistic Forecasting
lessons.interviewAnswer: A point forecast hides uncertainty. Probabilistic forecasting estimates quantiles or a full predictive distribution so decisions can reflect asymmetric risk and service levels.
keyPoints: Prediction interval includes future observation uncertainty.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Prediction Intervals & Probabilistic Forecasting make?

lessons.title: Machine Learning for Forecasting
lessons.interviewAnswer: Tree/boosting models can forecast by transforming temporal history into supervised features such as lags, rolling statistics, calendar variables and exogenous drivers. Backtesting must preserve temporal order and feature availability.
keyPoints: Global models can learn across many related series.
Recursive vs direct multi-step strategies differ.
Feature leakage is a major risk.

How would you validate or debug Machine Learning for Forecasting in practice?

lessons.title: Neural Forecasting
lessons.interviewAnswer: Neural forecasting models learn temporal patterns across one or many series using recurrent, convolutional or transformer-style architectures. They are most useful when scale, many related series or rich covariates justify the complexity.
keyPoints: Always compare with strong statistical baselines.
Global models share information across series.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Neural Forecasting make?
How would you validate or debug Neural Forecasting in practice?

lessons.title: Forecast Monitoring & Retraining
lessons.interviewAnswer: Forecast systems need monitoring for bias, scale changes, missing updates, driver drift and horizon-specific error. Retraining cadence should reflect how quickly relationships change and whether new labels arrive.
keyPoints: Bias can matter more than symmetric error.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Forecast Monitoring & Retraining make?
How would you validate or debug Forecast Monitoring & Retraining in practice?

lessons.title: Point, Contextual & Collective Anomalies
lessons.interviewAnswer: Anomalies can be unusual individual points, unusual only in context, or unusual sequences/groups. The detection method should match the anomaly definition rather than treating every extreme value as the same problem.
keyPoints: Context can be time, user, device or season.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Point, Contextual & Collective Anomalies make?
How would you validate or debug Point, Contextual & Collective Anomalies in practice?

lessons.title: Isolation Forest
lessons.interviewAnswer: Isolation Forest isolates observations through random feature splits; points requiring fewer splits are easier to isolate and receive more anomalous scores. It scales well for tabular unsupervised anomaly detection.
keyPoints: Contamination threshold maps scores to alerts.
Feature scaling is less central than distance-based methods but feature quality still matters.
lessons.labGoal: Detect unusual points without labels using Isolation Forest.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Isolation Forest make?
How would you validate or debug Isolation Forest in practice?

lessons.title: Local Outlier Factor & One-Class SVM
lessons.interviewAnswer: LOF compares local density with neighbors, while One-Class SVM learns a boundary around normal data. LOF captures local anomalies; One-Class SVM can be sensitive to scaling and hyperparameters.
keyPoints: Local methods struggle in high dimensions.
Thresholds should be calibrated to alert capacity.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Local Outlier Factor & One-Class SVM make?
How would you validate or debug Local Outlier Factor & One-Class SVM in practice?

lessons.title: Rare-event Evaluation & Alert Thresholds
lessons.interviewAnswer: For rare events, accuracy is usually misleading. Evaluate precision/recall, PR-AUC, recall at alert budget, expected cost and time-to-detection; choose thresholds based on operational capacity and error costs.
keyPoints: Time leakage is common in fraud/anomaly evaluation.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Rare-event Evaluation & Alert Thresholds make?
How would you validate or debug Rare-event Evaluation & Alert Thresholds in practice?

lessons.title: Censoring, Survival & Hazard Functions
lessons.interviewAnswer: Survival analysis models time until an event while handling censored observations whose event time is not fully observed. Survival S(t) is probability of surviving past t; hazard describes instantaneous event rate conditional on survival.
keyPoints: Do not treat censored durations as completed outcomes.
Hazard and survival encode related but different views.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Censoring, Survival & Hazard Functions make?
How would you validate or debug Censoring, Survival & Hazard Functions in practice?

lessons.title: Kaplan–Meier Estimator & Log-rank Test
lessons.interviewAnswer: Kaplan–Meier estimates the survival curve nonparametrically by multiplying conditional survival probabilities at event times. The log-rank test compares survival curves across groups under assumptions.
keyPoints: Median survival comes from S(t)=0.5 when reached.
Curves can cross, complicating simple comparisons.
lessons.labGoal: Fit and inspect a Kaplan–Meier survival curve.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Kaplan–Meier Estimator & Log-rank Test make?
How would you validate or debug Kaplan–Meier Estimator & Log-rank Test in practice?

lessons.title: Cox Proportional Hazards Model
lessons.interviewAnswer: The Cox model relates covariates multiplicatively to hazard without specifying the baseline hazard shape. Coefficients are interpreted through hazard ratios, under the proportional-hazards assumption.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Cox Proportional Hazards Model make?
How would you validate or debug Cox Proportional Hazards Model in practice?

lessons.title: Survival Model Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Survival models require metrics that handle censoring, such as concordance index and time-dependent calibration/Brier scores. Ordinary classification metrics at arbitrary cutoffs can discard useful time information.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Survival Model Evaluation make?
How would you validate or debug Survival Model Evaluation in practice?

lessons.title: Lagrange Multipliers, Duality & KKT Conditions
lessons.interviewAnswer: Lagrange multipliers incorporate constraints into an objective; KKT conditions characterize optima for broad constrained problems under regularity assumptions. Duality can provide bounds and alternative formulations.
keyPoints: Complementary slackness links active constraints and multipliers.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Lagrange Multipliers, Duality & KKT Conditions make?
How would you validate or debug Lagrange Multipliers, Duality & KKT Conditions in practice?

lessons.title: Linear Programming
lessons.interviewAnswer: Linear programming optimizes a linear objective under linear constraints. It is ideal for allocation, blending, planning and many operational decisions once predictions have been produced.
lessons.labGoal: Solve a small constrained allocation problem with linear programming.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Linear Programming make?
How would you validate or debug Linear Programming in practice?

lessons.title: Integer & Mixed-Integer Optimization
lessons.interviewAnswer: Integer programs require some decision variables to be discrete, enabling assignment, routing and scheduling but making optimization computationally harder than continuous LPs.
keyPoints: Formulation quality strongly affects solve time.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Integer & Mixed-Integer Optimization make?
How would you validate or debug Integer & Mixed-Integer Optimization in practice?

lessons.title: Bayesian Optimization for Expensive Objectives
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bayesian optimization fits a surrogate model of an expensive black-box objective and uses an acquisition function to choose promising evaluations, useful for costly hyperparameter or experiment tuning.
keyPoints: Best when evaluations are expensive, not huge-dimensional.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Bayesian Optimization for Expensive Objectives make?
How would you validate or debug Bayesian Optimization for Expensive Objectives in practice?

lessons.title: Recommender Baselines & Problem Formulation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Start with popularity, recency and simple content/history baselines. Define whether the task is rating prediction, top-N ranking, next-item prediction or candidate generation because metrics and data construction differ.
keyPoints: Negative samples are usually unobserved, not true dislikes.
Temporal splits better reflect recommendation deployment.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Recommender Baselines & Problem Formulation make?
How would you validate or debug Recommender Baselines & Problem Formulation in practice?

lessons.title: User–User & Item–Item Collaborative Filtering
lessons.interviewAnswer: Collaborative filtering recommends based on interaction similarity rather than item metadata. Item-item methods often provide stable neighborhood recommendations; user-user methods can suffer with sparse histories.
keyPoints: Cold start is a core limitation.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does User–User & Item–Item Collaborative Filtering make?
How would you validate or debug User–User & Item–Item Collaborative Filtering in practice?

lessons.title: Matrix Factorization for Recommenders
lessons.interviewAnswer: Matrix factorization learns low-dimensional user and item vectors whose interaction predicts preference. With implicit feedback, objectives often weight observed interactions plus sampled/unobserved examples.
keyPoints: Bias terms and confidence weighting matter.
lessons.labGoal: Factorize a tiny user-item rating matrix with gradient descent.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Matrix Factorization for Recommenders make?
How would you validate or debug Matrix Factorization for Recommenders in practice?

lessons.title: Candidate Generation vs Ranking
lessons.interviewAnswer: Large recommenders usually use a fast high-recall candidate stage followed by a richer ranking model. Candidate generation narrows millions of items; ranking uses more expensive features on hundreds/thousands.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Candidate Generation vs Ranking make?
How would you validate or debug Candidate Generation vs Ranking in practice?

lessons.title: Implicit Feedback & Negative Sampling
lessons.interviewAnswer: Clicks, views and purchases indicate exposure and preference imperfectly. Unobserved items are not necessarily negatives, so training often samples negatives or uses exposure-aware weighting.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Implicit Feedback & Negative Sampling make?
How would you validate or debug Implicit Feedback & Negative Sampling in practice?

lessons.title: Offline vs Online Recommender Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Offline ranking metrics measure historical predictive quality, but online experiments measure user/system impact. Historical logs are biased by the previous recommender, so offline gains do not guarantee online lift.
keyPoints: Use temporal splits and candidate consistency.
A/B tests capture behavior and feedback loops.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Offline vs Online Recommender Evaluation make?
How would you validate or debug Offline vs Online Recommender Evaluation in practice?

lessons.title: Diversity, Novelty, Coverage & Fairness in Recommenders
lessons.interviewAnswer: Recommender quality is broader than relevance. Diversity avoids redundant lists, novelty introduces useful less-obvious items, coverage distributes exposure, and fairness may constrain treatment of creators/users.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Diversity, Novelty, Coverage & Fairness in Recommenders make?
How would you validate or debug Diversity, Novelty, Coverage & Fairness in Recommenders in practice?

lessons.title: Inverted Index & Text Retrieval Pipeline
lessons.interviewAnswer: An inverted index maps terms to documents/postings containing them, making lexical search efficient. Real systems also tokenize, normalize, store term statistics and support field/position information.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Inverted Index & Text Retrieval Pipeline make?
How would you validate or debug Inverted Index & Text Retrieval Pipeline in practice?

lessons.title: TF-IDF & BM25
lessons.interviewAnswer: TF-IDF weights terms by within-document frequency and corpus rarity. BM25 adds saturation and document-length normalization, making it a strong lexical ranking baseline.
keyPoints: Lexical search handles exact names/codes well.
lessons.labGoal: Implement a tiny BM25 scorer and compare lexical ranking.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does TF-IDF & BM25 make?
How would you validate or debug TF-IDF & BM25 in practice?

lessons.title: MRR, MAP, Recall@K & NDCG
lessons.interviewAnswer: Retrieval metrics depend on whether you care about finding any relevant result, all relevant results, or graded relevance near the top. MRR emphasizes first relevant rank; NDCG rewards graded relevance with position discount.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does MRR, MAP, Recall@K & NDCG make?
How would you validate or debug MRR, MAP, Recall@K & NDCG in practice?

lessons.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
lessons.interviewAnswer: Exact vector search becomes expensive at large scale. ANN indexes trade a small amount of recall for much lower latency/memory cost using structures such as HNSW or IVF.
keyPoints: Distance metric must match embedding training/use.
lessons.labGoal: Build a small vector nearest-neighbor retrieval index.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search make?
How would you validate or debug Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in practice?

lessons.title: HNSW Intuition & Tuning
lessons.interviewAnswer: HNSW builds a multilayer proximity graph: upper sparse layers navigate quickly toward the neighborhood, and lower dense layers refine the search. Parameters trade build cost, memory, recall and latency.
keyPoints: efSearch trades query latency for recall.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does HNSW Intuition & Tuning make?
How would you validate or debug HNSW Intuition & Tuning in practice?

lessons.title: Hybrid Lexical + Vector Retrieval
lessons.interviewAnswer: Hybrid search combines lexical signals, which excel at exact terms and identifiers, with semantic vector similarity, which captures paraphrases. Scores can be normalized/fused or candidates reranked jointly.
keyPoints: Lexical and dense methods fail differently.
Reciprocal rank fusion is a simple robust fusion.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Hybrid Lexical + Vector Retrieval make?
How would you validate or debug Hybrid Lexical + Vector Retrieval in practice?

lessons.title: Cross-encoder / Learned Reranking
lessons.interviewAnswer: A reranker applies a more expensive query-document model to a small candidate set from first-stage retrieval. It improves precision because it jointly represents the query and candidate rather than comparing independent embeddings.
keyPoints: Use only on a bounded candidate set.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Cross-encoder / Learned Reranking make?
How would you validate or debug Cross-encoder / Learned Reranking in practice?

lessons.title: Text Normalization, Stemming & Lemmatization
lessons.interviewAnswer: Text normalization standardizes forms before classical NLP/search, but aggressive normalization can destroy meaning for names, code, languages or modern subword models.
keyPoints: Tokenization requirements depend on downstream model.
Stemming is heuristic; lemmatization uses linguistic forms.
Do not normalize IDs/code like prose.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Text Normalization, Stemming & Lemmatization make?
How would you validate or debug Text Normalization, Stemming & Lemmatization in practice?

lessons.title: Bag-of-Words, n-grams & TF-IDF
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bag-of-words represents term counts while n-grams add local order; TF-IDF downweights ubiquitous terms. These sparse representations remain strong, interpretable baselines for many text classification/search problems.
keyPoints: Linear models pair well with sparse features.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Bag-of-Words, n-grams & TF-IDF make?
How would you validate or debug Bag-of-Words, n-grams & TF-IDF in practice?

lessons.title: Word2Vec: Skip-gram & CBOW
lessons.interviewAnswer: Word2Vec learns dense word embeddings from context prediction. Skip-gram predicts context from a center word; CBOW predicts center from context, producing representations with useful distributional similarity.
keyPoints: Static word has one vector regardless of context.
Negative sampling approximates expensive softmax training.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Word2Vec: Skip-gram & CBOW make?
How would you validate or debug Word2Vec: Skip-gram & CBOW in practice?

lessons.title: RNNs, LSTMs & GRUs
lessons.interviewAnswer: RNNs process sequences recurrently but suffer long-range optimization issues; LSTM/GRU gates help preserve or forget state. Transformers largely replaced them for many NLP tasks but they remain important foundations and useful for some streaming sequences.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does RNNs, LSTMs & GRUs make?
How would you validate or debug RNNs, LSTMs & GRUs in practice?

lessons.title: Seq2Seq & Encoder–Decoder Attention
lessons.interviewAnswer: Encoder–decoder models map one sequence to another. Attention lets the decoder dynamically focus on encoder states instead of compressing the entire input into one fixed vector, paving the way for transformers.
keyPoints: Teacher forcing is common during training.
Exposure bias can appear at generation time.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Seq2Seq & Encoder–Decoder Attention make?
How would you validate or debug Seq2Seq & Encoder–Decoder Attention in practice?

lessons.title: Waveforms, Sampling Rate & Aliasing
lessons.interviewAnswer: Digital audio samples a continuous waveform at a fixed rate. Frequencies above the Nyquist limit cannot be represented correctly and can alias, so preprocessing and resampling need appropriate filtering.
keyPoints: Nyquist frequency is half sample rate.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Waveforms, Sampling Rate & Aliasing make?
How would you validate or debug Waveforms, Sampling Rate & Aliasing in practice?

lessons.title: STFT, Spectrograms & Mel Features
lessons.interviewAnswer: The short-time Fourier transform converts local waveform windows into time-frequency representations. Mel scaling compresses frequency resolution toward human perception and is common in speech features.
keyPoints: Window length trades time vs frequency resolution.
Magnitude/power and phase carry different information.
Log-Mel spectrograms are common ASR inputs.
lessons.labGoal: Convert a waveform into an STFT magnitude spectrogram.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does STFT, Spectrograms & Mel Features make?
How would you validate or debug STFT, Spectrograms & Mel Features in practice?

lessons.title: Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC)
lessons.interviewAnswer: CTC trains sequence models when input frames are much longer than output labels and exact alignments are unknown. It sums over valid alignments using blank/repeated-token rules.
keyPoints: Decoding can be greedy or beam search.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) make?
How would you validate or debug Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) in practice?

lessons.title: ASR Evaluation: WER & CER
lessons.interviewAnswer: Word Error Rate counts substitutions, deletions and insertions relative to reference word count. It is interpretable but can hide semantic differences and depends on text normalization conventions.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does ASR Evaluation: WER & CER make?
How would you validate or debug ASR Evaluation: WER & CER in practice?

lessons.title: OLTP vs OLAP
lessons.interviewAnswer: OLTP systems optimize many small transactional reads/writes with strong consistency; OLAP systems optimize scans and aggregations over large historical datasets. Modeling and storage choices differ because workloads differ.
keyPoints: Row-oriented often suits OLTP; columnar often suits analytics.
Do not run heavy analytical scans on critical transactional DBs.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does OLTP vs OLAP make?
How would you validate or debug OLTP vs OLAP in practice?

lessons.title: Star Schemas, Facts & Dimensions
lessons.interviewAnswer: A star schema separates measurable events in fact tables from descriptive entities in dimensions. Grain must be defined first; many analytical errors come from joining tables at inconsistent grain.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Star Schemas, Facts & Dimensions make?
How would you validate or debug Star Schemas, Facts & Dimensions in practice?

lessons.title: Slowly Changing Dimensions
lessons.interviewAnswer: SCD patterns define how dimension changes are represented. Type 1 overwrites history; Type 2 creates dated versions so historical facts can be analyzed with attributes valid at that time.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Slowly Changing Dimensions make?
How would you validate or debug Slowly Changing Dimensions in practice?

lessons.title: dbt: Transformation-as-Code
lessons.interviewAnswer: dbt manages SQL transformations as versioned models with dependencies, tests, documentation and incremental strategies inside the warehouse. It separates data transformation logic from extraction/loading infrastructure.
keyPoints: Tests protect assumptions such as uniqueness/not-null.
Incremental models need correct update keys/windows.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does dbt: Transformation-as-Code make?
How would you validate or debug dbt: Transformation-as-Code in practice?

lessons.title: Data Contracts, Lineage & Semantic Consistency
lessons.interviewAnswer: Data contracts make schemas, ownership and expectations explicit; lineage shows downstream dependencies. Together they reduce silent breakage and clarify impact when producers change data.
keyPoints: Schema compatibility is not enough; semantics matter.
Owners and SLAs should be explicit.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Data Contracts, Lineage & Semantic Consistency make?
How would you validate or debug Data Contracts, Lineage & Semantic Consistency in practice?

lessons.title: Partitioning & Sharding
lessons.interviewAnswer: Partitioning divides data/work across machines so systems scale. A good partition key balances load and supports common access patterns; skew creates hot partitions.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Partitioning & Sharding make?
How would you validate or debug Partitioning & Sharding in practice?

lessons.title: Replication & Consistency Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: Replication improves availability/read scale but creates questions about when replicas agree. Strong, eventual and session-level consistency offer different latency/availability trade-offs.
keyPoints: Read-after-write may matter even when global strong consistency does not.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Replication & Consistency Models make?
How would you validate or debug Replication & Consistency Models in practice?

lessons.title: CAP Theorem Without the Myth
lessons.interviewAnswer: Under a network partition, a distributed system must choose between always returning a consistent response and always remaining available. CAP is about partition scenarios, not a permanent “pick two” product label.
keyPoints: Partition tolerance is unavoidable in distributed networks.
Consistency has multiple definitions beyond CAP.
Latency trade-offs also matter outside partitions.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does CAP Theorem Without the Myth make?
How would you validate or debug CAP Theorem Without the Myth in practice?

lessons.title: Consensus & Leader Election
lessons.interviewAnswer: Consensus lets nodes agree on ordered decisions despite failures. Protocols such as Raft/Paxos use quorums and leaders/terms to coordinate replicated state machines.
keyPoints: Consensus solves metadata/control problems, not every data workload.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Consensus & Leader Election make?
How would you validate or debug Consensus & Leader Election in practice?

lessons.title: MapReduce, Shuffle & Distributed Aggregation
lessons.interviewAnswer: MapReduce partitions map work, groups intermediate keys through a shuffle, then reduces grouped values. Modern engines generalize this DAG model, but shuffle remains a major network/disk cost.
keyPoints: Map is embarrassingly parallel; shuffle is expensive.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does MapReduce, Shuffle & Distributed Aggregation make?
How would you validate or debug MapReduce, Shuffle & Distributed Aggregation in practice?

lessons.title: Retries, Idempotency & Exactly-once Semantics
lessons.interviewAnswer: Distributed operations fail partially. Retries are safe only when operations are idempotent or deduplicated. “Exactly once” usually means carefully defined processing/commit semantics rather than packets literally delivered once.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Retries, Idempotency & Exactly-once Semantics make?
How would you validate or debug Retries, Idempotency & Exactly-once Semantics in practice?

lessons.title: Design an Experimentation Platform
lessons.interviewAnswer: An experimentation platform needs deterministic assignment, exposure logging, metric computation, statistical analysis, guardrails, metadata and trustworthy diagnostics such as SRM. Separate experiment execution from analysis so decisions are reproducible.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Design an Experimentation Platform make?
How would you validate or debug Design an Experimentation Platform in practice?

lessons.title: Design a Forecasting Platform
lessons.interviewAnswer: A forecasting platform must ingest time-indexed data, define cutoffs/horizons, construct leakage-safe features, run rolling backtests, train/version models, generate probabilistic forecasts and monitor bias/accuracy by segment.
keyPoints: Backtest and production feature pipelines must match.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Design a Forecasting Platform make?
How would you validate or debug Design a Forecasting Platform in practice?

lessons.title: Design a Search / Retrieval System
lessons.interviewAnswer: A search system typically has document ingestion/indexing, query understanding, first-stage lexical/vector retrieval, optional reranking, caching and offline/online evaluation. The design should state latency, freshness and relevance objectives.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions does Design a Search / Retrieval System make?
How would you validate or debug Design a Search / Retrieval System in practice?

lessons.title: Norms, Distances & Similarity
lessons.interviewAnswer: Norms measure vector magnitude; distance functions measure separation; similarity functions such as cosine compare direction. The choice changes model geometry, nearest neighbors, clustering and regularization.
keyPoints: L1 and L2 norms behave differently.
Distance concentration becomes problematic in high dimensions.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Norms, Distances & Similarity have?
How would you validate Norms, Distances & Similarity on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Orthogonality, Projections & Least Squares
lessons.interviewAnswer: Least squares can be understood as projecting the target vector onto the column space of the design matrix; the residual is orthogonal to that space at the optimum.
keyPoints: Rank deficiency makes solutions non-unique without additional choices.
QR/SVD are numerically preferable to explicit matrix inverse.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Orthogonality, Projections & Least Squares have?
How would you validate Orthogonality, Projections & Least Squares on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Jacobians, Hessians & Second-order Thinking
lessons.interviewAnswer: The Jacobian collects first derivatives of vector-valued functions; the Hessian contains second derivatives of a scalar objective and describes local curvature.
keyPoints: Second-order methods can converge quickly but are expensive in high dimensions.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Jacobians, Hessians & Second-order Thinking have?
How would you validate Jacobians, Hessians & Second-order Thinking on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Numerical Stability: log-sum-exp, overflow & conditioning
lessons.interviewAnswer: Mathematically equivalent formulas can behave very differently in floating point. Stable implementations avoid overflow/underflow, poor conditioning and subtractive cancellation.
keyPoints: Avoid explicit matrix inversion when solves/decompositions are available.
Scale values and inspect NaN/Inf early.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Numerical Stability: log-sum-exp, overflow & conditioning have?
How would you validate Numerical Stability: log-sum-exp, overflow & conditioning on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions
lessons.interviewAnswer: A joint distribution describes variables together; marginalization sums/integrates out variables; conditioning updates the distribution given observed information.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions have?
How would you validate Joint, Marginal & Conditional Distributions on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Independence & Conditional Independence
lessons.interviewAnswer: Independence means the joint factorizes into marginals; conditional independence means two variables become independent after conditioning on a third set. Conditional independence is central to graphical models and causal reasoning.
keyPoints: Zero correlation does not generally imply independence.
Conditioning can remove or create dependence.
DAG separation statements are about conditional independence.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Independence & Conditional Independence have?
How would you validate Independence & Conditional Independence on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Monte Carlo Simulation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Monte Carlo approximates expectations or probabilities with repeated random samples. Error typically shrinks with the square root of sample count, so simulation is flexible but can be computationally expensive.
keyPoints: Use simulation when analytic calculation is hard.
Random seeds improve reproducibility, not statistical validity.
lessons.labGoal: Estimate a probability with Monte Carlo simulation.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Monte Carlo Simulation have?
How would you validate Monte Carlo Simulation on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Law of Total Probability & Total Expectation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Condition on useful groups, solve within each group, then average using group probabilities. These identities are powerful for mixture distributions, debugging aggregate metrics and Bayesian reasoning.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Law of Total Probability & Total Expectation have?
How would you validate Law of Total Probability & Total Expectation on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Database Normalization: 1NF to 3NF
lessons.interviewAnswer: Normalization reduces update anomalies by separating facts according to functional dependencies; analytical systems may deliberately denormalize for read performance.
keyPoints: Know the grain/key of every table.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Database Normalization: 1NF to 3NF have?
How would you validate Database Normalization: 1NF to 3NF on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Query Plans & SQL Performance
lessons.interviewAnswer: A query optimizer chooses scans, joins and access paths based on statistics and indexes. Explain plans reveal whether a slow query is scanning too much, joining badly or missing useful indexes/partition pruning.
keyPoints: Index presence does not guarantee index use.
Predicate pushdown and partition pruning reduce data read.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Query Plans & SQL Performance have?
How would you validate Query Plans & SQL Performance on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Transactions & Isolation Levels
lessons.interviewAnswer: Isolation levels trade concurrency against anomalies such as dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms. Serializable provides the strongest familiar abstraction but may cost throughput/retries.
keyPoints: MVCC is a common implementation technique.
Application invariants may require stronger handling than default isolation.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Transactions & Isolation Levels have?
How would you validate Transactions & Isolation Levels on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Columnar Storage, Parquet & Predicate Pushdown
lessons.interviewAnswer: Columnar formats store values by column, enabling compression and selective scans for analytics. Parquet also stores metadata/statistics that engines can use for predicate pushdown and row-group pruning.
keyPoints: Columnar is ideal for scans of a subset of columns.
Compression benefits from similar adjacent values.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Columnar Storage, Parquet & Predicate Pushdown have?
How would you validate Columnar Storage, Parquet & Predicate Pushdown on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Lakehouse
lessons.interviewAnswer: Warehouses emphasize managed structured analytics; data lakes store flexible files/objects; lakehouse approaches add table metadata, transactions and governance over object storage. The right choice depends on workload and organizational needs.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Lakehouse have?
How would you validate Warehouse vs Data Lake vs Lakehouse on a real dataset?

lessons.title: LDA & QDA
lessons.interviewAnswer: Linear and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis model class-conditional Gaussian distributions. LDA shares covariance across classes and yields linear boundaries; QDA allows class-specific covariance and quadratic boundaries.
keyPoints: Generative classifiers model p(x|y) and priors.
LDA lower variance; QDA more flexible.
Covariance estimation can be unstable in high dimensions.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does LDA & QDA have?
How would you validate LDA & QDA on a real dataset?

lessons.title: AdaBoost
lessons.interviewAnswer: AdaBoost sequentially focuses new weak learners on examples previous learners misclassified, then combines learners with performance-based weights. It illustrates boosting before gradient-boosted trees.
keyPoints: Weak learners combine into strong ensemble.
Sensitive to noisy labels/outliers in some settings.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does AdaBoost have?
How would you validate AdaBoost on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Probability Calibration
lessons.interviewAnswer: A classifier is calibrated when predictions of 0.8 correspond to about 80% positive outcomes among comparable cases. Ranking metrics can be strong while probabilities are badly calibrated.
lessons.labGoal: Measure and improve probability calibration.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Probability Calibration have?
How would you validate Probability Calibration on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Decision Thresholds & Cost-sensitive Classification
lessons.interviewAnswer: The default 0.5 threshold is arbitrary unless costs and class priors justify it. Choose thresholds using validation data, business costs, safety constraints or capacity targets.
keyPoints: Changing threshold changes precision/recall, not underlying ranking.
Tune after training on held-out data.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Decision Thresholds & Cost-sensitive Classification have?
How would you validate Decision Thresholds & Cost-sensitive Classification on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Regression Metrics: RMSE, MAE, MAPE & R²
lessons.interviewAnswer: Regression metrics emphasize different error properties. RMSE punishes large errors; MAE is robust and in target units; MAPE fails near zero and weights relative errors unevenly; R² measures variance explained relative to a mean baseline.
