followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Regression Metrics: RMSE, MAE, MAPE & R² have?
How would you validate Regression Metrics: RMSE, MAE, MAPE & R² on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Scaling & Encoding Features
lessons.interviewAnswer: Scaling matters for distance- and gradient-based models; categorical encoding choices affect leakage, dimensionality and generalization. Tree models often need less scaling but still require correct category handling.
keyPoints: One-hot is robust for low-cardinality nominal categories.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Scaling & Encoding Features have?
How would you validate Scaling & Encoding Features on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Interactions & Domain Feature Engineering
lessons.interviewAnswer: Feature engineering can expose known structure—ratios, interactions, lags, log transforms or domain aggregations—especially for simpler models. Every feature must be available at prediction time.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Interactions & Domain Feature Engineering have?
How would you validate Interactions & Domain Feature Engineering on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Change-point Detection
lessons.interviewAnswer: Change-point detection looks for structural shifts in a sequence—mean, variance or distribution changes—rather than isolated anomalous points. It is useful for regime changes, deployments and sensor failures.
keyPoints: Control false alarms vs detection delay.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Change-point Detection have?
How would you validate Change-point Detection on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Supervised Rare-event Modeling
lessons.interviewAnswer: When rare-event labels exist, treat the problem as cost-sensitive classification with careful temporal splits, sampling/weighting and precision-recall evaluation rather than unsupervised anomaly detection.
keyPoints: Calibrate/adjust probabilities if training distribution changes.
Use event-time split to avoid leakage.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Supervised Rare-event Modeling have?
How would you validate Supervised Rare-event Modeling on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Accelerated Failure Time Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: AFT models describe how covariates accelerate or decelerate event time directly, offering an alternative interpretation to proportional hazards models.
keyPoints: Models a distribution of log survival time.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Accelerated Failure Time Models have?
How would you validate Accelerated Failure Time Models on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Competing Risks
lessons.interviewAnswer: Competing risks occur when multiple mutually exclusive event types can happen and one prevents observation of another. Treating competing events as ordinary censoring can misestimate event probabilities.
keyPoints: Cause-specific hazard and cumulative incidence answer different questions.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Competing Risks have?
How would you validate Competing Risks on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Multi-objective Optimization & Pareto Trade-offs
lessons.interviewAnswer: Many real systems optimize several conflicting objectives. Pareto-optimal solutions cannot improve one objective without worsening another; teams often scalarize objectives or impose constraints/guardrails.
keyPoints: Weighted sums encode preferences but can hide trade-offs.
Constraints are often clearer for safety/SLA requirements.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Multi-objective Optimization & Pareto Trade-offs have?
How would you validate Multi-objective Optimization & Pareto Trade-offs on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Cold Start in Recommender Systems
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cold start happens when new users/items lack interaction history. Content features, onboarding signals, exploration and popularity/context priors bridge the gap until collaborative signals accumulate.
keyPoints: User and item cold start differ.
Avoid trapping new items behind popularity bias.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Cold Start in Recommender Systems have?
How would you validate Cold Start in Recommender Systems on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Learning to Rank: Pointwise, Pairwise & Listwise
lessons.interviewAnswer: Learning-to-rank objectives optimize ordering rather than only class labels. Pointwise treats items independently, pairwise compares preferences, and listwise objectives model the ranked list more directly.
keyPoints: Training objective should align with ranking metric.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Learning to Rank: Pointwise, Pairwise & Listwise have?
How would you validate Learning to Rank: Pointwise, Pairwise & Listwise on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Query Understanding: Spelling, Intent & Filters
lessons.interviewAnswer: Search quality often improves before retrieval by normalizing queries, correcting spelling, identifying entities/intent and extracting structured filters. Query rewriting must preserve user intent.
keyPoints: Exact identifiers should not be “corrected” like prose.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Query Understanding: Spelling, Intent & Filters have?
How would you validate Query Understanding: Spelling, Intent & Filters on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Named Entity Recognition & Sequence Labeling
lessons.interviewAnswer: NER assigns labels such as person, organization or product to token spans. Classical CRF/BiLSTM systems model label dependencies; modern transformers fine-tune contextual token representations.
keyPoints: Span-level F1 is more meaningful than token accuracy.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Named Entity Recognition & Sequence Labeling have?
How would you validate Named Entity Recognition & Sequence Labeling on a real dataset?

lessons.title: NLP Generation Metrics: BLEU, ROUGE & Beyond
lessons.interviewAnswer: BLEU measures n-gram precision with brevity handling, ROUGE emphasizes overlap/recall; both are limited proxies for semantic quality. Modern evaluation often combines task metrics, learned metrics and human judgment.
keyPoints: Lexical overlap can punish valid paraphrases.
Human/LLM evaluation needs rubrics and reliability checks.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does NLP Generation Metrics: BLEU, ROUGE & Beyond have?
How would you validate NLP Generation Metrics: BLEU, ROUGE & Beyond on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Text-to-Speech Pipeline
lessons.interviewAnswer: Modern TTS maps text/phonetic representations to acoustic features or latent speech and then uses a vocoder/decoder to synthesize waveform audio. Quality involves intelligibility, naturalness, speaker/style control and latency.
keyPoints: Acoustic model and vocoder are distinct conceptual stages.
Evaluate with human listening plus objective diagnostics.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Text-to-Speech Pipeline have?
How would you validate Text-to-Speech Pipeline on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Change Data Capture (CDC)
lessons.interviewAnswer: CDC captures inserts, updates and deletes from source systems so downstream stores can update incrementally without repeated full extracts. Log-based CDC is common for low-latency replication.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Change Data Capture (CDC) have?
How would you validate Change Data Capture (CDC) on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Event Time, Processing Time & Watermarks
lessons.interviewAnswer: Streaming systems distinguish when an event occurred from when it was processed. Watermarks express progress in event time and let systems close windows while tolerating bounded late data.
keyPoints: Watermark policy trades completeness vs latency.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Event Time, Processing Time & Watermarks have?
How would you validate Event Time, Processing Time & Watermarks on a real dataset?

lessons.title: CSV vs Parquet vs Avro
lessons.interviewAnswer: CSV is simple text but lacks strong types/efficient analytics; Parquet is columnar for analytical scans; Avro is row-oriented with schemas and is common for event serialization.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does CSV vs Parquet vs Avro have?
How would you validate CSV vs Parquet vs Avro on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Spark Shuffles, Partitions & Data Skew
lessons.interviewAnswer: Spark operations such as joins/groupBy can trigger shuffles that move data across workers. Poor partitioning or skewed keys create stragglers, spills and high network cost.
keyPoints: Salt/skew handling can spread hot keys.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions or limitations does Spark Shuffles, Partitions & Data Skew have?
How would you validate Spark Shuffles, Partitions & Data Skew on a real dataset?

lessons.title: Sampling Design: Random, Stratified & Cluster Sampling
lessons.interviewAnswer: Sampling design determines which population the data represents. Simple random sampling gives each unit equal probability; stratification samples within known groups; cluster sampling selects groups and can increase correlation/variance.
keyPoints: Sampling mechanism affects both bias and standard error.
Stratification can improve precision for important subgroups.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Sampling Design: Random, Stratified & Cluster Sampling?
How would you validate or tune Sampling Design: Random, Stratified & Cluster Sampling?

lessons.title: Selection, Coverage & Nonresponse Bias
lessons.interviewAnswer: More data does not fix a systematically unrepresentative sample. Selection and nonresponse bias occur when inclusion/response is related to the outcome or variables of interest.
keyPoints: Distinguish sampling variance from systematic bias.
Weighting can help only when selection is modeled with adequate information.
Instrumentation and eligibility define the population actually observed.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Selection, Coverage & Nonresponse Bias?
How would you validate or tune Selection, Coverage & Nonresponse Bias?

lessons.title: Grid, Random & Bayesian Hyperparameter Search
lessons.interviewAnswer: Hyperparameter tuning searches settings not learned directly by model fitting. Random search is often more efficient than exhaustive grids in high-dimensional spaces; Bayesian optimization helps when evaluations are expensive.
keyPoints: Tune using validation/CV, never the final test set.
Search spaces matter more than search algorithm in many cases.
Parallelism and early stopping can reduce cost.
lessons.labGoal: Tune a model without touching the test set.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Grid, Random & Bayesian Hyperparameter Search?
How would you validate or tune Grid, Random & Bayesian Hyperparameter Search?

lessons.title: Nested Cross-validation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Nested cross-validation separates hyperparameter/model selection in an inner loop from unbiased performance estimation in an outer loop. It is useful when datasets are small and tuning would otherwise contaminate evaluation.
keyPoints: Inner CV selects; outer CV estimates.
Final deployment can refit after evaluation protocol is complete.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Nested Cross-validation?
How would you validate or tune Nested Cross-validation?

lessons.title: Bagging, Blending & Stacking
lessons.interviewAnswer: Ensembling combines diverse models to reduce error. Bagging averages models trained on resampled data; stacking learns a meta-model from out-of-fold predictions; blending uses a held-out set.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Bagging, Blending & Stacking?
How would you validate or tune Bagging, Blending & Stacking?

lessons.title: Permutation Importance, PDP & SHAP
lessons.interviewAnswer: Interpretability tools answer different questions: permutation importance measures performance drop when a feature is disrupted; PDP shows average predicted response; SHAP attributes prediction differences under a chosen background/assumption framework.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Permutation Importance, PDP & SHAP?
How would you validate or tune Permutation Importance, PDP & SHAP?

lessons.title: Dashboard & BI Design
lessons.interviewAnswer: A good dashboard starts from decisions and questions, not chart availability. Use stable metric definitions, clear filters/time windows, meaningful comparisons and enough context to distinguish signal from normal variation.
keyPoints: One screen should have a clear decision purpose.
Show denominators, time grain and targets/baselines.
Avoid mixing metric definitions across pages.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Dashboard & BI Design?
How would you validate or tune Dashboard & BI Design?

lessons.title: Data Storytelling & Communicating Uncertainty
lessons.interviewAnswer: Data storytelling means structuring evidence around the decision: context, key finding, uncertainty, alternatives and recommended action. It is not decorating charts or hiding caveats.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Data Storytelling & Communicating Uncertainty?
How would you validate or tune Data Storytelling & Communicating Uncertainty?

lessons.title: Image Preprocessing & Data Augmentation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Image preprocessing standardizes model inputs; augmentation creates plausible label-preserving variation to improve generalization. Augmentations must respect task semantics—horizontal flips are not universally valid.
keyPoints: Validation/test data should not receive stochastic training augmentation.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Image Preprocessing & Data Augmentation?
How would you validate or tune Image Preprocessing & Data Augmentation?

lessons.title: Transfer Learning & Fine-tuning in Vision
lessons.interviewAnswer: Transfer learning starts from pretrained visual features and adapts them to a target task. With limited data, freeze more layers initially; with enough domain data, fine-tune carefully using smaller learning rates and validation.
keyPoints: Head-only training is a baseline, not a law.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Transfer Learning & Fine-tuning in Vision?
How would you validate or tune Transfer Learning & Fine-tuning in Vision?

lessons.title: Object Detection: Boxes, Anchors & Modern Detectors
lessons.interviewAnswer: Object detection predicts both classes and locations. Two-stage detectors separate proposals and classification; one-stage detectors predict densely. Modern detectors may be anchor-based or anchor-free, but all require localization and classification reasoning.
keyPoints: Bounding-box regression and classification are separate losses/signals.
NMS or set-prediction logic resolves duplicate detections.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Object Detection: Boxes, Anchors & Modern Detectors?
How would you validate or tune Object Detection: Boxes, Anchors & Modern Detectors?

lessons.title: IoU, NMS & mAP for Detection
lessons.interviewAnswer: Intersection-over-Union measures box overlap; Non-Maximum Suppression removes redundant overlapping predictions; mAP summarizes precision-recall across classes and IoU thresholds depending on benchmark.
keyPoints: IoU threshold defines a localization match.
NMS threshold affects duplicate vs missed close objects.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use IoU, NMS & mAP for Detection?
How would you validate or tune IoU, NMS & mAP for Detection?

lessons.title: Segmentation Metrics: IoU, Dice & Pixel Accuracy
lessons.interviewAnswer: Pixel accuracy can be misleading when background dominates. IoU and Dice emphasize overlap between predicted and true masks; per-class metrics reveal minority-structure performance.
keyPoints: Dice is closely related to F1 on pixels.
Boundary metrics can matter for thin structures.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Segmentation Metrics: IoU, Dice & Pixel Accuracy?
How would you validate or tune Segmentation Metrics: IoU, Dice & Pixel Accuracy?

lessons.title: Self-supervised & Contrastive Visual Representation Learning
lessons.interviewAnswer: Self-supervised vision learns representations from unlabeled images using objectives such as contrastive agreement or masked reconstruction, then transfers them to downstream tasks.
keyPoints: Large diverse pretraining data can reduce label needs.
Linear-probe vs fine-tune evaluate representation quality differently.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Self-supervised & Contrastive Visual Representation Learning?
How would you validate or tune Self-supervised & Contrastive Visual Representation Learning?

lessons.title: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN)
lessons.interviewAnswer: GCNs aggregate normalized neighbor features and transform them layer by layer, creating node representations that mix local graph structure and attributes. Repeated aggregation can oversmooth representations.
lessons.labGoal: Implement one normalized GCN propagation step with NumPy.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN)?
How would you validate or tune Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN)?

lessons.title: Graph Attention Networks (GAT)
lessons.interviewAnswer: GAT learns attention weights over neighbors so different neighbors contribute differently instead of using fixed aggregation weights.
keyPoints: Attention is local over graph neighbors.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Graph Attention Networks (GAT)?
How would you validate or tune Graph Attention Networks (GAT)?

lessons.title: Heterogeneous Graphs & Relation Types
lessons.interviewAnswer: Heterogeneous graphs contain different node/edge types whose relations have different semantics. Models often use relation-specific transformations or metapath/message-passing strategies.
keyPoints: Reverse edges are often explicit for directed relation flow.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Heterogeneous Graphs & Relation Types?
How would you validate or tune Heterogeneous Graphs & Relation Types?

lessons.title: Graph-level Prediction & Pooling
lessons.interviewAnswer: For graph-level tasks, node embeddings must be aggregated into a graph representation using mean/sum/max, attention or hierarchical pooling before prediction.
keyPoints: Sum/mean pooling encode different size behavior.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Graph-level Prediction & Pooling?
How would you validate or tune Graph-level Prediction & Pooling?

lessons.title: Simpson’s Paradox & Aggregation Bias
lessons.interviewAnswer: A trend can reverse after stratifying by a confounding/grouping variable because aggregate weights differ. Always inspect important segments before interpreting an overall association.
keyPoints: Different group composition can reverse comparisons.
Causal conclusions need more than stratification alone.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Simpson’s Paradox & Aggregation Bias?
How would you validate or tune Simpson’s Paradox & Aggregation Bias?

lessons.title: Interference & Network Effects in Experiments
lessons.interviewAnswer: Standard A/B inference assumes one unit’s treatment does not change another unit’s outcome. Social, marketplace and collaborative products violate this through interference, requiring cluster designs or specialized estimands.
keyPoints: Cluster randomization reduces contamination but changes power.
followUpQuestions: When would you not use Interference & Network Effects in Experiments?
How would you validate or tune Interference & Network Effects in Experiments?

lessons.title: Data Observability: Freshness, Volume, Schema & Distribution
lessons.interviewAnswer: Data observability monitors pipeline outputs beyond job success: freshness, volume, schema, nulls, distribution and lineage. A pipeline can be green while silently producing wrong data.
keyPoints: Baseline distributions and contracts catch silent shifts.
Route alerts to owners with context/lineage.

visualSummaries.title: Data Observability: Freshness, Volume, Schema & Distribution

followUpQuestions: When would you not use Data Observability: Freshness, Volume, Schema & Distribution?
How would you validate or tune Data Observability: Freshness, Volume, Schema & Distribution?

lessons.title: Entropy & Information Content
lessons.interviewAnswer: Entropy measures average uncertainty in a distribution: concentrated distributions have low entropy; balanced, unpredictable distributions have higher entropy.
followUpQuestions: Why use a logarithm?
How is entropy related to compression?

lessons.title: Cross-Entropy & Log Loss
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cross-entropy evaluates a predicted probability distribution against the target. In classification it rewards high probability on the true class and heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions.
followUpQuestions: Cross-entropy vs KL divergence?
Why train on logits?

lessons.title: KL Divergence
lessons.interviewAnswer: KL divergence measures how poorly distribution Q approximates P. It is non-negative but asymmetric, so it is not a distance metric.
followUpQuestions: Why does KL appear in VAEs?
Forward vs reverse KL?

lessons.title: Mutual Information
lessons.interviewAnswer: Mutual information measures how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about another and can capture nonlinear dependence.
followUpQuestions: MI vs correlation?
Conditional mutual information?

lessons.title: Perplexity
lessons.interviewAnswer: Perplexity is the exponential of average negative log-likelihood. Lower is better on the same data/tokenization, but perplexity is not directly comparable across different tokenizers.
followUpQuestions: Bits-per-character?
Why can lower perplexity fail downstream?

lessons.title: Information Bottleneck & Representation Learning
lessons.interviewAnswer: The information-bottleneck view seeks representations that preserve information useful for a target while discarding irrelevant detail.
followUpQuestions: How does this relate to VAEs/VQ models?
Compression vs fidelity?

lessons.title: Gaussian Processes
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Gaussian process defines a distribution over functions using a mean and kernel; conditioning on observations produces a posterior predictive distribution with both mean and uncertainty.
followUpQuestions: What does the kernel control?
How do sparse GPs scale?

lessons.title: Bayesian Networks & d-Separation
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Bayesian network is a DAG that factorizes a joint distribution into local conditional distributions; d-separation encodes conditional-independence relationships.
followUpQuestions: Bayesian network vs MRF?
Exact vs approximate inference?

lessons.title: Markov Random Fields & Factor Graphs
lessons.interviewAnswer: An MRF is an undirected graphical model whose joint distribution is expressed with local compatibility factors; it is useful when dependencies are symmetric rather than naturally directed.
followUpQuestions: What is a factor graph?
Why is the partition function hard?

lessons.title: Hidden Markov Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: An HMM models a sequence with hidden states that follow Markov transitions and emit observations. Forward-backward computes marginals/likelihoods, Viterbi finds the most likely state path, and Baum–Welch learns parameters.
followUpQuestions: Forward-backward vs Viterbi?
How is Baum–Welch related to EM?

lessons.title: Variational Inference
lessons.interviewAnswer: Variational inference converts difficult posterior inference into optimization: choose a tractable q(z) and optimize it to approximate the true posterior, commonly by maximizing the ELBO.
followUpQuestions: Mean-field VI?
Why reverse KL?

lessons.title: Aleatoric vs Epistemic Uncertainty
lessons.interviewAnswer: Aleatoric uncertainty comes from irreducible data noise; epistemic uncertainty comes from limited model knowledge and can often be reduced with better data.
followUpQuestions: How do ensembles help?
What happens under shift?

lessons.title: Proper Scoring Rules: Log Loss & Brier Score
lessons.interviewAnswer: Proper scoring rules reward honest probabilistic forecasts: in expectation, reporting the true probability minimizes expected score. Log loss and Brier score are common examples.
followUpQuestions: Brier vs log loss?
Calibration vs discrimination?

lessons.title: Conformal Prediction
lessons.interviewAnswer: Conformal prediction wraps a predictive model to output sets or intervals with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability; a calibration set determines the nonconformity-score quantile.
lessons.labGoal: Build split-conformal regression intervals from held-out residuals.
followUpQuestions: What assumptions are needed?
Conditional vs marginal coverage?

lessons.title: Selective Prediction & Abstention
lessons.interviewAnswer: Selective prediction lets a model abstain on uncertain cases, trading coverage—the fraction answered—against risk on the answered subset.
followUpQuestions: How do you choose the abstention threshold?
How does conformal prediction help?

lessons.title: Empirical Risk Minimization
lessons.interviewAnswer: ERM minimizes average training loss; generalization theory asks when low empirical risk also implies low expected risk on unseen data.
followUpQuestions: What controls the generalization gap?
How does regularization modify ERM?

lessons.title: PAC Learning Intuition
lessons.interviewAnswer: PAC learning formalizes whether enough samples let a learner find, with high probability, a hypothesis whose true error is approximately small.
followUpQuestions: Realizable vs agnostic PAC?
How does VC dimension enter?

lessons.title: VC Dimension & Capacity
lessons.interviewAnswer: VC dimension measures the richness of a binary hypothesis class via the largest set of points it can shatter; greater capacity usually requires more data for uniform generalization guarantees.
followUpQuestions: What does shatter mean?
How does VC dimension affect sample complexity?

lessons.title: Margins & Generalization
lessons.interviewAnswer: A classification margin measures separation from the decision boundary; large-margin methods such as SVMs prefer a wider buffer while allowing controlled violations in the soft-margin case.
followUpQuestions: Hard vs soft margin?
How do kernels change geometry?

lessons.title: Regularization as Capacity Control
lessons.interviewAnswer: Regularization penalizes or constrains effective model complexity, often trading a little training fit for better generalization when variance is high.
followUpQuestions: Explicit vs implicit regularization?
How does λ change bias/variance?

lessons.title: Generalization Under Distribution Shift
lessons.interviewAnswer: IID test performance can fail under covariate, label or concept shift. Use time/geography/group-aware validation, shift diagnostics and post-deployment monitoring when future data differs from training.
followUpQuestions: How do you detect shift?
When does importance weighting help?

lessons.title: Frequent Itemsets & Association Rules
lessons.interviewAnswer: Association-rule mining finds frequent item combinations and rules A→B. Support measures frequency, confidence estimates P(B|A), and lift compares the rule with B’s baseline rate.
followUpQuestions: Apriori vs FP-Growth?
Why is support anti-monotonic?

lessons.title: MinHash & Jaccard Similarity
lessons.interviewAnswer: MinHash creates compact signatures whose collision probability equals Jaccard similarity, allowing approximate set similarity at scale.
followUpQuestions: How does MinHash connect to LSH?
How many hashes are enough?

lessons.title: Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH)
lessons.interviewAnswer: LSH intentionally hashes similar items into the same buckets with high probability, reducing candidates for approximate similarity or nearest-neighbor search.
followUpQuestions: LSH vs HNSW?
How do bands affect recall?

lessons.title: Bloom Filters
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Bloom filter is a compact probabilistic set-membership structure: it can return false positives but not false negatives under normal insert/query use.
followUpQuestions: How do k and array size affect false positives?
Counting Bloom filter?

lessons.title: Count-Min Sketch & Heavy Hitters
lessons.interviewAnswer: Count-Min Sketch approximates frequencies in streams with multiple hash tables; queries take the minimum counter and overestimate nonnegative frequencies within probabilistic error bounds.
followUpQuestions: How do you recover heavy-hitter keys?
Count-Min vs hash map?

lessons.title: HyperLogLog & Distinct Counting
lessons.interviewAnswer: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements from hashed leading-zero statistics, giving low relative error with very small memory and easy merging.
followUpQuestions: Why is HLL mergeable?
How does memory affect error?

lessons.title: PageRank & Link Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: PageRank scores nodes by the stationary distribution of a random walk with teleportation: links from important nodes contribute more than raw in-degree alone.
followUpQuestions: PageRank vs HITS?
How does damping affect ranking?

lessons.title: Vector vs Raster Spatial Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: Vector data represents discrete geometry as points, lines and polygons; raster data represents space as a grid of cells. The correct representation depends on the phenomenon and operations.
followUpQuestions: When would you rasterize polygons?
How do vector indexes work?

lessons.title: Coordinate Reference Systems & Projections
lessons.interviewAnswer: A CRS defines how coordinates map to Earth. Longitude/latitude is angular; projected CRSs map locations to a plane for meaningful distance/area calculations over a suitable region.
followUpQuestions: What is EPSG:4326?
Which projection for area?

lessons.title: Spatial Joins & Predicates
lessons.interviewAnswer: A spatial join combines rows based on geometric relations such as within, contains, intersects or nearest instead of equality on a key.
followUpQuestions: sjoin vs nearest?
How do indexes accelerate joins?

lessons.title: Spatial Indexes, Geohash & H3
lessons.interviewAnswer: Spatial indexes reduce expensive geometry comparisons by pruning candidates. R-trees organize bounding boxes; hierarchical grids such as geohash/H3 encode locations into cells.
followUpQuestions: R-tree vs H3?
How does indexing help kNN?

lessons.title: Geodesic Distance & Spatial kNN
lessons.interviewAnswer: Global spatial distance should respect Earth geometry or use an appropriate projection; raw Euclidean distance on latitude/longitude can be misleading.
followUpQuestions: Geodesic vs routing distance?
How would you accelerate spatial kNN?

lessons.title: Spatial Autocorrelation & Moran’s I
lessons.interviewAnswer: Spatial autocorrelation asks whether nearby observations are more similar than expected. Moran’s I is a common global measure; local indicators identify spatial clusters/outliers.
followUpQuestions: Global vs local Moran?
Effect on regression?

lessons.title: Spatial Cross-Validation & Geographic Leakage
lessons.interviewAnswer: Random splits can overestimate geospatial model performance because nearby samples are correlated; spatial blocking or leave-region-out validation better measures transfer to new areas.

visualSummaries.title: Spatial validation holds out coherent regions

followUpQuestions: How choose block size?
Spatial vs temporal leakage?

lessons.title: Causal Masks vs Bidirectional Attention
lessons.interviewAnswer: Causal masks prevent tokens from attending to future positions for autoregressive next-token prediction; bidirectional encoders can attend to both sides under different objectives.
followUpQuestions: How does BERT differ?
How does masking interact with KV cache?

lessons.title: Cross-Attention
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cross-attention uses queries from one sequence and keys/values from another, letting one representation retrieve information from a different encoder or modality.
followUpQuestions: Cross-attention vs concatenation?
Where does diffusion use it?

lessons.title: RoPE & Modern Positional Encoding
lessons.interviewAnswer: RoPE rotates query/key feature pairs according to token position so relative position affects attention scores without simply adding a fixed position vector.
followUpQuestions: RoPE vs ALiBi?
Why Q/K rather than V?

lessons.title: Mixture-of-Experts Transformers
lessons.interviewAnswer: MoE layers route each token to a small subset of expert feed-forward networks, increasing total model capacity without activating all parameters per token.
followUpQuestions: Dense vs MoE inference cost?
What is expert collapse?

lessons.title: LLM Training Lifecycle: Pretraining → SFT → Preference Tuning
lessons.interviewAnswer: Modern LLM development commonly starts with next-token pretraining, then supervised instruction fine-tuning, and may add preference optimization such as RLHF or DPO. Each stage serves a different purpose.
followUpQuestions: SFT vs continued pretraining?
RLHF vs DPO?

lessons.title: Topic Modeling & LDA
lessons.interviewAnswer: Latent Dirichlet Allocation is a probabilistic topic model where documents are mixtures of latent topics and topics are distributions over words.
followUpQuestions: How choose number of topics?
LDA vs embedding clustering?

lessons.title: Text Classification & Encoder Fine-tuning
lessons.interviewAnswer: A pretrained text encoder can be fine-tuned with a classification head or used as a frozen embedding extractor. Fine-tuning adapts more strongly but costs more and can overfit small data.
followUpQuestions: Fine-tune vs embeddings + linear model?
Which metric for imbalance?

lessons.title: Feature Stores: Offline vs Online
lessons.interviewAnswer: A feature store manages reusable feature definitions and provides historical point-in-time-correct features for training plus fresh low-latency values for online inference.
followUpQuestions: When is a feature store overkill?
Batch vs streaming features?

lessons.title: Training–Serving Skew
lessons.interviewAnswer: Training-serving skew occurs when feature or preprocessing semantics differ between offline training and live inference because of code, time, freshness or source differences.
followUpQuestions: How test offline/online parity?
How does point-in-time correctness help?

lessons.title: Data, Model & Experiment Lineage
lessons.interviewAnswer: ML lineage records which data snapshot, feature definitions, code commit, configuration, environment and artifact produced a model version so it can be reproduced and audited.
followUpQuestions: What belongs in a model registry?
How do containers help?

lessons.title: ML Testing & Quality Gates
lessons.interviewAnswer: ML systems need software tests plus data/model checks such as schema invariants, leakage tests, slice metrics, baseline comparison, latency bounds and deployment gates.
followUpQuestions: Unit vs integration tests?
How test nondeterministic training?

lessons.title: Kernel Methods & the Kernel Trick
lessons.interviewAnswer: Kernel methods replace an explicit nonlinear feature map with a kernel that computes inner products in that feature space, enabling algorithms such as SVMs to learn nonlinear boundaries without materializing all transformed features.
followUpQuestions: What makes a kernel valid?
RBF vs polynomial?
Why do kernel methods scale poorly with n?

lessons.title: Perceptron & Online Learning
lessons.interviewAnswer: The perceptron is an online linear classifier that updates weights only when an example is misclassified. Under linear separability it has a finite mistake bound tied to the margin.

lessons.title: Factor Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: Factor analysis models observed variables as linear combinations of a smaller number of latent factors plus variable-specific noise, focusing on shared covariance structure.

lessons.title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
lessons.interviewAnswer: ICA decomposes observed mixtures into latent components that are statistically independent, typically relying on non-Gaussianity; unlike PCA, the objective is independence rather than just uncorrelated variance directions.

lessons.title: Time-Series Foundation Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: Time-series foundation models pretrain on large collections of sequences and adapt or zero-shot forecast new series. They can reduce per-series modeling work, but still need comparison with strong naive/statistical baselines and careful domain-shift evaluation.
